item.title: Whose Economy Are We Building? Rethinking Preference in Nigerian Public Procurement
item.dc:creator: Kelechi Uzoma Obijiaku
item.description: Why government contracts could do more for women, persons with disabilities and the communities that fund them
item.content:encoded:
Why government contracts could do more for women, persons with disabilities and the communities that fund them

Something about the way we discuss domestic preference in Nigerian public procurement has always interested me.

The conventional argument is that government should give some advantage to Nigerian businesses when they compete against foreign suppliers. That makes sense in appropriate circumstances, particularly where international competitive bidding is involved. But the reality is that a significant proportion of procurement opportunities at the state and local government levels are already contested among Nigerian businesses.

So, what exactly are we achieving by discussing domestic preference almost exclusively in terms of Nigerian versus foreign suppliers?

Perhaps we should be asking a different question: Can public procurement be used more deliberately to expand economic opportunities for people and communities that have historically struggled to access them?

I think this is a conversation Nigeria needs to have.

Preference doesn't always mean favouritism

In February 2026, Nigeria's Bureau of Public Procurement announced a collaborative initiative with the International Trade Centre and Korea's Public Procurement Service to strengthen understanding of affirmative procurement. The proposed national policy is intended to improve opportunities for groups including women, young people and persons with disabilities.

This is an encouraging development, particularly because affirmative procurement is no longer an entirely unfamiliar concept in Nigeria.

Kaduna has introduced measures to expand procurement opportunities for women-owned businesses, while Lagos announced the approval of a gender-responsive procurement framework in 2025, including a minimum allocation of 10% of eligible contracts to women-owned enterprises.

These initiatives reflect an important recognition: treating everyone identically in a procurement process does not necessarily mean everyone has an equal opportunity to compete.

Consider a woman-owned business with the technical competence to execute a government contract but limited access to finance, previous government contracts or the extensive documentation sometimes demanded during qualification. Or an entrepreneur with a disability who encounters inaccessible procurement platforms and administrative procedures.

Removing those barriers, simplifying appropriate requirements and providing targeted opportunities may achieve more than simply announcing that procurement is open to everyone.

And where the applicable law permits, a modest preference margin or carefully designed reservation can help make participation more meaningful.

What if states took this further?

Now consider another possibility.

A state government awards billions of naira in contracts annually. Yet many of the businesses executing those contracts may have little economic presence in the communities where the projects are located.

Could the government design procurement incentives that encourage bidders to establish genuine local operations, employ residents, train young people or source suitable materials from businesses within the state?

For example, imagine a state introducing a modest, transparently disclosed evaluation advantage for qualified contractors that commit to employing a defined proportion of residents on a labour-intensive project. Alternatively, a contractor could earn recognition for establishing a functioning local service centre, providing apprenticeships or subcontracting appropriate portions of work to capable local SMEs.

These are not necessarily the same as excluding businesses from other states. A company headquartered in Abuja could still compete for a contract in Lagos, employ Lagos residents and establish the facilities required to deliver the project effectively.

The emphasis would be on measurable economic contribution rather than ancestry.

And there is a potentially important distinction here. A preference based on genuine local employment or service-delivery capacity may be easier to justify than one based simply on whether the business owner is considered an indigene.

The constitutional question cannot be ignored

Nigeria's Constitution protects citizens against discrimination on grounds including ethnic group, community and place of origin. Section 42 is particularly relevant, while Section 15 emphasises national integration and the need to promote a sense of belonging among Nigerians.

Consequently, any proposal to reserve public contracts exclusively for state indigenes would raise serious constitutional questions.

This is especially important in a country where conversations about indigeneity, residence and ethnic identity can become politically sensitive.

But there is room for a more thoughtful policy discussion.

Rather than asking where a company's owners originally come from, governments could examine whether the business contributes to the economy of the state through employment, skills development, genuine operational presence and local supply-chain participation.

Even these measures would require a proper legal basis, objective criteria and careful assessment of their effects on competition. A local-office requirement, for instance, should not become an artificial barrier designed to favour established contractors.

A better approach might permit successful bidders to establish the necessary presence after award, where that is sufficient for effective contract performance.

The distinction is subtle, but important.

Government can seek to develop its local economy without turning public procurement into an instrument of ethnic exclusion.

But who pays for the preference?

There is, of course, another side to this discussion.

Every procurement preference has a potential cost. If government accepts a higher evaluated price to achieve a social or economic objective, that additional expenditure must be justified.

A preference should therefore be modest, legally authorised, transparently disclosed and connected to measurable public benefits. It should never excuse poor technical competence, unacceptable quality or failure to deliver.

There is also the familiar risk of fronting. A business could claim to be women-owned, disability-inclusive or locally established without the intended beneficiaries exercising genuine ownership, control or receiving meaningful economic benefits.

Verification, beneficial-ownership checks, contract monitoring and periodic evaluation would be essential.

Perhaps most importantly, governments should measure outcomes rather than merely count preferential awards. How many sustainable jobs were created? Did participating businesses grow? Were contracts successfully completed? Did the intervention improve access without substantially undermining competition?

Those questions should determine whether a preference continues, changes or ends.

A different way of looking at value for money

We often measure procurement success through the price paid and the quality of goods, works or services delivered. Those considerations remain fundamental.

But public expenditure can also generate wider economic benefits when procurement policies are carefully designed.

A contract that delivers a functioning public facility while developing local technical capacity, expanding opportunities for women-owned enterprises or creating sustainable employment may produce benefits that extend beyond the immediate project.

That does not mean every social objective belongs in every tender. Procurement must remain competitive, accountable and commercially sensible.

It does suggest, however, that governments should think more deliberately about the economic outcomes their purchasing decisions can produce.

Nigeria's emerging affirmative procurement conversation offers an opportunity to do exactly that.

Perhaps the future of domestic preference should not be limited to protecting Nigerian businesses from foreign competition. It could also involve creating fairer opportunities within Nigeria itself.

And for state governments, the question may be even more immediate.

When we spend public money, are we simply purchasing goods and services, or are we also building the economic capacity of the people and communities we serve?

I think we can do both, provided we are thoughtful about how we go about it.

item.title: When a Company Gets Blacklisted: The Hidden Cost of Procurement Misconduct
item.dc:creator: Kelechi Uzoma Obijiaku
item.description: Imagine a company spending years building its contracting business. It acquires equipment, hires capable people, delivers projects and earns the confidence of its clients.
item.content:encoded:
Imagine a company spending years building its contracting business. It acquires equipment, hires capable people, delivers projects and earns the confidence of its clients.

Then one procurement investigation changes the conversation.

Suddenly, future tenders are in doubt. A prospective joint-venture partner wants explanations. The compliance team is looking through old bid documents, and management is asking how long the company might be excluded from government business.

The immediate sanction may not be the most expensive part. The real cost could be the contracts the company will never get the chance to compete for.

That is why I think supplier debarment deserves more attention than it usually receives.

Nigeria has just made the conversation particularly relevant.

Nigeria's new enforcement push

In October 2026, Nigeria's Bureau of Public Procurement announced the enforcement of a national guideline under which contractors, consultants and service providers may face exclusion from federal procurement for three to five years for specified misconduct.

The reported grounds include bribery, falsified documents, fraudulent conduct and wilful or persistent failure to perform contractual obligations. A prior sanction by a multilateral development institution may also be considered.

What interests me is the connection between integrity and actual contract performance. Debarment is not only about a corrupt bidding process. A contractor that repeatedly fails to deliver may also create a serious risk for public expenditure.

But there is an important legal distinction. Section 58(6) of Nigeria's Public Procurement Act 2007 separately prescribes, upon conviction of a corporate offender, debarment for not less than five years together with a financial penalty. That statutory consequence should not be casually confused with the administrative periods described in the new guideline.

Different legal routes require careful attention to their respective conditions and safeguards.

The UK's risk-based approach

In the United Kingdom, the Procurement Act 2023 has established a central debarment framework. The Debarment Review Service, now within the Government Commercial Agency, investigates suppliers for possible inclusion on the published list; the final decision rests with a Minister.

The distinction between mandatory and discretionary exclusion matters. Some listed suppliers must generally be excluded from covered procurements; in other cases, authorities retain discretion, subject to proper assessment and justification.

Perhaps the more interesting point is the philosophy behind the system. The UK's guidance treats debarment as a measure for managing continuing or recurring supplier risk, rather than simply a punishment for historical wrongdoing.

Has the company addressed the conduct? Have its controls improved? Is the risk likely to recur?

Those are more useful questions than merely asking whether something went wrong five years ago.

When misconduct crosses borders

The World Bank's list of ineligible firms and individuals shows why this issue is no longer confined to one jurisdiction.

Under the cross-debarment arrangements among participating multilateral development banks, certain sanctions may be recognised by other institutions, subject to the agreement's rules. A company sanctioned in one development-finance setting can therefore face consequences for opportunities elsewhere.

That does not mean every allegation or every national blacklisting automatically produces a worldwide ban. The legal basis and scope of each sanction still matter.

Nevertheless, for suppliers bidding on donor-funded infrastructure, energy, technology or consulting projects, the commercial implications are obvious.

Compliance is part of business strategy

There is a practical lesson here for both sides of the procurement table.

Suppliers need to know what their agents promise, what their subcontractors do and whether the representations in their bids can actually be supported. They should document conflicts of interest, maintain reliable performance records and investigate credible complaints before those complaints become a crisis.

Procurement authorities, meanwhile, need more than a spreadsheet of blacklisted names. They need dependable evidence, clear procedures, opportunities for suppliers to respond, proportionate decisions and a credible route for review or rehabilitation where the applicable rules permit it.

Otherwise, a safeguard intended to protect public money could become a mechanism for arbitrary exclusion.

This is particularly important in African procurement markets, where supplier capacity is sometimes limited and government remains a major purchaser. Excluding a supplier can protect the public interest, but doing so carelessly can also reduce competition and invite litigation.

One final thought

We often treat procurement compliance as a legal department's problem, something to address after a complaint arrives.

I see it differently.

A company's eligibility to compete for future business is itself a valuable commercial asset. Protecting that asset requires honest bidding, reliable delivery, sound internal controls and management that takes warning signs seriously.

A contract won through misconduct may look profitable today. The opportunities lost tomorrow could make it the most expensive contract the company ever secured.

And that is a cost no sensible business should ignore.

item.title: THE CHEAPEST BID CAN BECOME THE MOST EXPENSIVE CONTRACT
item.dc:creator: Kelechi Uzoma Obijiaku
item.description: There's something about the lowest bid that makes it particularly attractive.
item.content:encoded:
There's something about the lowest bid that makes it particularly attractive.

For a procurement officer, it can be reassuring. For an accounting officer, it may appear financially prudent. And for an auditor reviewing the procurement process several months later, the decision might seem perfectly reasonable.

After all, if one contractor offers to execute a project for ₦800 million while another quotes ₦950 million, why should government spend an additional ₦150 million?

It's a fair question. But here's another question we don't ask often enough.

What if the ₦800 million contract eventually costs ₦1.3 billion? And what if the contractor who quoted ₦950 million could have delivered the same project within budget, on schedule and to the required standard?

Suddenly, the cheapest bid doesn't look particularly cheap anymore.

This is one of the more interesting contradictions in public procurement. We spend considerable time establishing procedures to ensure that government obtains competitive prices. Yet, sometimes, we pay insufficient attention to what happens after the contract has been awarded. And that is where the real cost of procurement often emerges.

The difference between price and value

Let me clarify something. There is absolutely nothing wrong with awarding a contract to the lowest bidder.

In fact, where bids satisfy the applicable responsiveness, qualification and evaluation requirements, selecting the lowest evaluated responsive bid can be entirely appropriate. The problem arises when we confuse the lowest quoted price with the lowest overall cost. They are not necessarily the same thing.

Consider a contractor who submits an unusually low bid to secure a government project. Six months into implementation, the contractor begins experiencing cash-flow difficulties. Materials become more expensive. Progress slows. Requests for variations start arriving.

Eventually, the project requires additional funding, an extension of time or, in particularly unfortunate circumstances, termination and reprocurement.

The original contract price may have been competitive. The eventual procurement outcome certainly wasn't.

This is why international procurement practice emphasises value for money, appropriate evaluation methodologies and consideration of costs over the relevant life cycle. The World Bank's Procurement Regulations for IPF Borrowers, for example, recognise that value for money involves more than simply obtaining the lowest initial price. The objective is to achieve an appropriate balance of quality, cost and other relevant considerations.

But procurement officers are not fortune-tellers

One difficulty with this conversation is that procurement professionals cannot predict every future development. Exchange rates fluctuate. Inflation changes. Supply chains become disrupted. Governments sometimes delay payments.

Even a perfectly capable contractor can encounter difficulties that were not reasonably foreseeable when the contract was awarded.

So, the solution cannot simply be to reject every unusually low bid or automatically select a more expensive contractor. That would create another problem entirely.

Instead, procurement institutions need evaluation systems capable of distinguishing between genuinely competitive pricing and pricing that creates unacceptable delivery risks. Depending on the applicable procurement rules and the nature of the contract, this may involve examining price realism, technical methodology, financial capacity, implementation schedules and life-cycle costs.

The important point is that these considerations must be incorporated transparently into the procurement process, rather than introduced arbitrarily after bids have been received. Procurement discretion must remain accountable.

The contract award is not the finish line

There is another dimension to this issue that deserves attention. Even where the right contractor is selected through a properly conducted procurement process, value for money can still disappear during contract implementation.

Poorly drafted contracts, inadequate supervision, weak performance indicators and uncontrolled variations can undermine an otherwise successful procurement exercise. This is why I believe contract management deserves significantly more institutional attention.

Think about it. An organisation may spend months developing procurement plans, preparing tender documents, evaluating bids and obtaining the necessary approvals. Yet, once the contract is signed, the same level of discipline is not always sustained.

Contract management is sometimes treated as a largely administrative exercise involving payment certificates, progress reports and correspondence. But effective contract management should be much more than that.

It should involve continuous monitoring of contractual obligations, early identification of emerging risks, verification of deliverables, management of variations and timely intervention when performance begins to deteriorate. The objective is not merely to establish whether the contractor has complied with the agreement. It is to ensure that the organisation actually receives the value it contracted to obtain.

What this means for Nigeria and other developing economies

For countries facing significant infrastructure deficits and competing demands on public resources, the consequences of poor procurement outcomes are particularly serious. Every abandoned project, avoidable cost escalation or poorly performing contract represents resources that could have been deployed elsewhere.

This makes the relationship between procurement evaluation and contract management especially important. We need procurement systems that encourage genuine competition without rewarding commercially unrealistic promises.

We also need institutions that understand that contract administration is not something to worry about only when disputes arise. It begins with the way the procurement itself is designed.

Clear specifications, realistic delivery timelines, appropriate risk allocation, measurable performance standards and well-considered payment structures can all influence whether a contract succeeds. And procurement professionals should be involved in these conversations from the beginning.

A final thought

Perhaps we need to become a little less impressed by how much money a procurement exercise appears to have saved at the point of contract award. A lower contract price is certainly worth celebrating. But the more meaningful question is whether those savings survive implementation.

Did the contractor deliver? Was the project completed within the agreed parameters? Did the organisation receive the required quality? And, ultimately, was public money well spent?

Because the true cost of procurement is not always the figure written on the contract award letter. Sometimes, it is the amount we eventually pay to correct the consequences of getting the procurement wrong.

And that is why the cheapest bid can occasionally become the most expensive contract.

Kelechi Obijiaku writes Procure2save, exploring public procurement, contract management, commercial law and institutional reform.

item.title: WHEN GOVERNMENTS SAY “BUY LOCAL”, WHO REALLY WINS?
item.dc:creator: Kelechi Uzoma Obijiaku
item.description: Something interesting is happening in international public procurement, and I think we should be paying closer attention to it, particularly here in Africa.
item.content:encoded:
Something interesting is happening in international public procurement, and I think we should be paying closer attention to it, particularly here in Africa.

For years, the conversation around public procurement has largely centred on transparency, competition, fairness and value for money. Open up the market, allow qualified suppliers to compete, evaluate their bids fairly and award contracts in accordance with established rules.

Fair enough.

But governments are increasingly asking another question. Why should billions in public expenditure not also be used to strengthen domestic industries, protect jobs and build national economic capacity?

And interestingly, this conversation is no longer confined to developing economies.

On 9 September 2026, the European Commission unveiled a proposal for a new Public Procurement Act. The proposed legislation would replace the existing procurement directives with a single regulation, simplify procurement procedures and introduce a stronger European preference framework.

In other words, Europe is considering how to use its enormous public procurement market more deliberately to support European businesses and industries.

Now, here's where things get interesting.

The proposal goes beyond merely encouraging governments to purchase European products. It also seeks to integrate environmental sustainability, innovation, security and supply-chain resilience into procurement decisions.

Under the proposed framework, quality-related criteria would generally account for at least 30% of evaluation weighting, rising to 50% for labour-intensive contracts, subject to an alternative approach where contracting authorities explain how quality is otherwise assured.

There is also a proposal for a connected digital procurement marketplace across the European Union.

Of course, this is still proposed legislation. It requires approval by the European Parliament and Council, with the institutions working towards adoption by the end of 2027.

But the direction is quite revealing.

Public procurement is increasingly being treated not simply as an administrative mechanism for purchasing goods and services, but as an instrument of economic and industrial policy.

And that brings me to Nigeria.

Our Nigeria First policy similarly seeks to prioritise Nigerian-made goods and capable indigenous businesses in government procurement. In his 2026 budget address, President Tinubu emphasised the policy's role in supporting local industries, creating employment and reducing dependence on imports.

Only last week, on 22 October, the Presidency again highlighted this policy while discussing opportunities for indigenous engineering companies in Nigeria's oil and gas industry.

So, in a sense, Nigeria and Europe are confronting a similar policy question, although from very different economic positions.

How do we use government purchasing power to develop our domestic economies without undermining competition, quality and efficiency?

I find this particularly interesting because public procurement has always involved more than simply purchasing things.

When a government awards a contract for the construction of a hospital, for instance, it is purchasing infrastructure. But that expenditure can also create employment, support local manufacturers, develop technical expertise and strengthen domestic supply chains.

The question is whether the procurement system is deliberately designed to achieve these additional benefits.

However, there's a catch.

Local preference policies can become counterproductive if they are poorly implemented.

Imagine a government restricting competition in favour of domestic suppliers without first establishing whether those suppliers possess the necessary technical capacity, financial strength or production capability.

What happens when delivery fails?

Or when protected suppliers become less competitive because they know that government contracts are practically guaranteed?

We could end up protecting inefficiency rather than promoting industrial development.

And I think this is where procurement professionals, commercial lawyers and policymakers have an important responsibility.

A properly designed local content policy should not simply favour domestic businesses. It should help them become genuinely competitive.

That means developing transparent eligibility criteria, verifying local value addition, encouraging technology transfer, strengthening supplier development programmes and measuring actual contract performance.

It also means distinguishing between a genuinely indigenous manufacturer and a company that merely imports finished products, changes the packaging and presents them as locally manufactured.

Both may be legally registered domestic businesses, but their contributions to industrial development are hardly the same.

There are commercial law implications too.

Local content requirements must be properly reflected in tender documents and contractual obligations. Otherwise, how do we enforce commitments relating to local employment, technology transfer or domestic sourcing?

And where international trade commitments apply, procurement preferences must be carefully structured to remain legally defensible.

I would also argue that African countries should think beyond their individual national markets.

If every African government pursues local preference without considering regional supply chains, we risk creating fragmented markets that are too small to support competitive industries.

Perhaps there is room for a more coordinated African approach, where domestic industrial development and regional trade reinforce rather than undermine each other.

After all, a Nigerian manufacturer that becomes competitive enough to supply public institutions in Ghana, Kenya or Rwanda has achieved something considerably more valuable than merely securing preferential access to contracts at home.

The European proposal has reminded me of something important.

Public procurement is not just about how governments spend money. It is also about what those spending decisions make possible.

The challenge is ensuring that our pursuit of economic sovereignty does not become an excuse for inefficiency, protectionism or reduced accountability.

Because buying local should ultimately help us build businesses capable of competing globally.

Otherwise, what exactly are we protecting?

item.title: LOCAL CONTENT AND THE COST QUESTION IN NIGERIA
item.dc:creator: Kelechi Uzoma Obijiaku
item.description: Nigeria likes the language of local content. It appears in speeches, policy papers, industrial plans, reform discussions and procurement conversations across government. The idea behind it is easy to understand and even easier to support. If the State spends enormous sums each year on goods, works and services, that spending should do more than meet immediate needs. It should also help build domestic industry, support jobs, deepen technical capacity and keep more value within the local economy.
item.content:encoded:
Nigeria likes the language of local content. It appears in speeches, policy papers, industrial plans, reform discussions and procurement conversations across government. The idea behind it is easy to understand and even easier to support. If the State spends enormous sums each year on goods, works and services, that spending should do more than meet immediate needs. It should also help build domestic industry, support jobs, deepen technical capacity and keep more value within the local economy.

That instinct is sound. Public procurement is not a routine back-office activity. It is one of the most consequential economic tools available to government. When the State buys at scale, it does not merely acquire roads, buildings, medicines, power infrastructure or digital systems. It shapes markets. It influences which firms expand, which sectors attract investment, which suppliers gain confidence, and which productive capacities begin to take root.

That point matters even more in a country like Nigeria, where the scale of public expenditure is too large to ignore. Once government is spending in the trillions, procurement decisions stop being narrow administrative choices. They become economic signals. Over time, they can either reinforce domestic production or leave local firms stranded at the margins of supply chains they ought to be participating in.

That is where local content enters the conversation. But it is also where the conversation becomes difficult.

It is easy to endorse local content in principle. It becomes harder when one is sitting in an actual bid opening or evaluation session. A procuring entity is reviewing offers for a road project, a housing development, a hospital, a public building, or an energy-related installation. The technical threshold has been crossed. The bidders are substantially responsive. Then the financial offers are opened and the numbers tell an awkward story. The bid built around imported inputs is cheaper. The bid that relies more heavily on local materials or local manufacturing comes in higher.

At that point, nobody is speaking in abstract policy slogans anymore. The question becomes immediate and practical. Should public funds follow the lower evaluated price, or should government absorb some additional cost in the name of developing domestic industry?

That is the real local content dilemma in Nigeria. The country wants to produce more at home, but the conditions under which local firms operate often make local production more expensive than imported alternatives.

It is important to pause here and resist the lazy conclusion. The fact that imported goods are sometimes cheaper does not automatically prove that Nigerian manufacturers are inefficient. Nor does it mean local content policy is naïve or economically unsound. In many cases, the difference in price has less to do with effort or competence and more to do with the structure of production itself.

The first issue is scale. Manufacturing economies do not gain advantage merely because they produce. They gain advantage because they produce at volume and within systems that reward volume. When output is large enough, fixed costs begin to behave differently. Machinery, tooling, compliance overhead, plant administration, research costs and other long-run investments are spread across vast numbers of units. That alone can drive down unit cost in ways that smaller manufacturing environments cannot easily match.

China remains the clearest illustration of this. Its manufacturing strength was never just about cheap labour. It was built on dense industrial clusters, reliable supporting infrastructure, supplier ecosystems, coordinated logistics and output levels that transformed cost structures. Vietnam offers another useful example. Its manufacturing base has grown within an environment where industrial production became central to the economy rather than peripheral to it. These are the kinds of production settings against which a fragmented and still-maturing industrial base must compete.

Nigeria, by contrast, is still trying to build that level of industrial coherence. There are promising clusters, particularly around Lagos and Ogun, and there is no shortage of entrepreneurial energy. But scale is still uneven. In many sectors, domestic production remains too fragmented to produce the kind of cost efficiencies that large industrial economies take for granted. That gap inevitably shows up in procurement pricing.

The second issue is energy. This point has almost become too familiar in discussions about Nigerian manufacturing, yet it remains central. Stable electricity is not an optional convenience in industrial production. It is part of the cost foundation. Where power supply is reliable, firms can plan more accurately, reduce wastage, run production cycles efficiently and price with greater certainty. Where it is not, they are forced to generate their own stability at enormous expense.

That cost does not disappear. It travels. It moves from diesel tanks and alternative power arrangements into the price of finished goods. By the time a local manufacturer submits a bid, the burden of unstable power has already been priced in. It is therefore misleading to compare a locally produced item with an imported one without taking account of the radically different cost environments from which each emerged.

The third issue is logistics. Production is not just about making things. It is also about moving them. Raw materials must reach factories. Finished products must reach warehouses, markets and project sites. In more efficient production environments, roads, ports, rail, warehousing and distribution systems work with reasonable predictability. Delays are reduced, losses are contained, and transport costs are manageable. In Nigeria, logistics still impose a serious commercial penalty. Port delays, inland haulage costs, warehousing burdens and general distribution inefficiencies all push costs upward. A manufacturer may be technically capable and commercially serious, yet still struggle to compete simply because the journey from input to output is too expensive.

The fourth issue is finance. Industrial growth is capital-hungry. Machinery must be purchased, facilities expanded, working capital maintained, and production cycles funded. Where long-term finance is available at reasonable cost, firms can invest, grow and recover expenses over time in a way that keeps pricing competitive. Where finance is costly, the burden reappears in the final product price. A manufacturer cannot borrow expensively, operate in a high-cost environment and then pretend those costs do not exist when tendering. They will surface somewhere, and they usually surface in the bid price.

Once these factors are taken together, the so-called paradox begins to look less mysterious. The imported product is not always cheaper because the foreign producer is uniquely brilliant and the local producer is not. Often, it is cheaper because it comes from a production environment built on scale, lower financing costs, steadier power and more efficient logistics, while the Nigerian manufacturer is operating within a much harsher commercial setting.

This leaves procurement professionals in a genuinely difficult position. Procurement law and practice are right to insist on value for money. Public officers are stewards of scarce public resources. Oversight bodies, auditors and approving authorities are entitled to ask whether government obtained the most economically advantageous outcome. That discipline exists for a reason and should not be casually discarded.

At the same time, governments often expect procurement to do more than purchase efficiently. They expect it to serve wider public goals. In many developing economies, that includes supporting domestic industry, encouraging local participation, building jobs and reducing long-term dependence on imports. Those objectives are not irrational. In fact, they are entirely legitimate. The trouble begins when they collide with immediate price realities.

That is why domestic preference provisions exist. Nigeria’s procurement framework allows room, in appropriate circumstances, for preference in favour of domestic goods and contractors. That is not accidental. It reflects a policy judgment that the lowest price in the short term is not always the choice with the highest public value over time. If a country wants to build productive capacity, procurement cannot remain blind to that objective.

But preference has limits. It can soften the edge of a structural disadvantage, not erase it. It can help a local bidder remain competitive at evaluation stage, but it cannot solve poor power supply, fragmented production, expensive capital or weak logistics. In other words, preference can buy time, but it cannot manufacture competitiveness.

This is why the experience of the oil and gas sector remains so instructive. It shows that local content becomes meaningful when procurement is tied to regulation, market certainty and deliberate capacity development. The success recorded in that space did not happen because the country merely repeated the phrase "local content" often enough. It happened because demand was backed by rules, participation was structured, and local firms were given room to grow around a framework that signalled seriousness over time.

There is a lesson there for other sectors. If government wants local content to succeed beyond rhetoric, it cannot rely solely on occasional preference during tender evaluation. That is far too late in the cycle. By the time tenders are being scored, the structural disadvantages have already done their work. The more serious question is how government can create the conditions under which local suppliers become genuinely competitive before bids are submitted.

That is where procurement planning deserves far more respect than it usually receives. Too often, procurement plans are treated as compliance paperwork, prepared because they are required and filed because they must exist. But procurement planning can do much more than satisfy an administrative rule. It can act as a demand signal. If ministries, departments and agencies are likely to purchase similar categories of goods across a financial year or across a medium-term horizon, that demand should not remain invisible and scattered. Where it can be coordinated, aggregated or at least signalled with some predictability, suppliers can plan around it.

That matters because manufacturers do not invest on the strength of patriotic speeches. They invest when demand appears credible, sustained and commercially meaningful. If government demand is fragmented, irregular, poorly timed or inconsistent from one agency to another, local firms will struggle to justify expansion. They will remain too small to benefit from scale, and the price gap between local and imported goods will remain stubbornly wide.

Framework agreements, coordinated procurement, forward demand signalling and category-based planning can therefore do more for local content than occasional declarations of preference. Repeated and predictable demand gives domestic firms a basis for investment. Investment can support expansion. Expansion can produce scale. Scale can lower costs. At that point, local content begins to move from aspiration to market reality.

This, in truth, is the more serious conversation. The question is not simply whether Nigeria should buy local. The deeper question is how government can help create the conditions in which buying local ceases to attract a constant cost penalty.

Procurement alone cannot carry that burden. Power must improve. Transport and industrial logistics must improve. Access to affordable finance must improve. Standards, testing infrastructure and quality assurance must also improve, because competitiveness is not measured by price alone. Reliability matters. Consistency matters. Delivery matters. Performance matters. A local firm that wins only because it is local, but cannot supply at the required quality or pace, does not strengthen local content. It undermines confidence in it.

That is why local content should never be treated as a permanent shelter from competition. It should be treated as a bridge to competitiveness. The objective is not to create a procurement culture in which government pays more indefinitely merely to prove a political point. The objective is to help domestic suppliers reach a stage where they can compete on price, quality, delivery and reliability without special indulgence.

Once that happens, the procurement officer is no longer trapped between policy and price. The local supplier wins not because the system has bent over backwards to protect it, but because it offers genuine value. That is the point at which local content stops looking like a difficult compromise and begins to look like sound economics.

Nigeria has not fully arrived there yet. That much is clear. But the fact that the country is still confronting this tension should not lead to cynicism or policy fatigue. It should lead to better alignment. Procurement policy, industrial policy, infrastructure planning, energy reform and access to finance cannot keep moving in separate directions while the country expects local content to succeed by force of sentiment alone.

If those areas begin to work together, the local content conversation will gradually change. The question will no longer be whether government should tolerate a premium to support domestic industry. The better question will be how quickly domestic industry can meet public demand competitively and at scale.

That is where Nigeria needs to get to. Not a country that merely speaks eloquently about local content, but one that can buy confidently from industries that are genuinely ready to supply it.
